blocks.text: The surrounding passage identifies Cyrus as the agent through whom God will bring Babylon’s defeat, Jerusalem’s restoration, and the release of exiles. Calling him God’s “anointed” does not depict him as an Israelite Davidic king; it presents him as an instrument used for Israel’s restoration. Questions about how this material relates to the formation of the received book of Isaiah remain debated.

The invitation to “all the ends of the earth” in verses 20–25 belongs within Isaiah’s wider portrayal of nations and empires: they may be judged and held accountable, yet the book also envisages nations learning, worshiping, and participating in restoration. Here the contrast is between powerless idols and the one God who saves, ending with universal homage to that God.

Isaiah 45:23 later echoes in Philippians’ portrayal of God highly exalting the Messiah and granting the name associated with universal homage and confession. Readers interpret the relationship in different ways: proposed backgrounds include Isaianic, Adamic, imperial, wisdom, and divine-identity readings, and no single source is established by the available evidence. This distinction matters because moving from the later letter’s confession to a developed doctrinal system is a further interpretive step.
